stem: How did President Clinton respond to the Republican victory of 1994?

options.text: He moved toward the center, declaring the era of big government over
He vetoed every bill the Republican Congress passed for the rest of his presidency
options.misconception: Clinton signed major Republican-backed measures, including welfare reform in 1996.

options.text: He resigned from the presidency rather than work with a Republican Congress
options.misconception: Clinton served out both terms and won reelection in 1996.

options.text: He called for the repeal of the Contract with America by constitutional amendment
options.misconception: Clinton never proposed a constitutional amendment against the Contract; he co-opted its agenda instead.

rationales.A: Background: Clinton declared the era of big government over, embraced NAFTA and welfare reform, and stole Republican thunder — a shift that helped him win reelection in 1996.
rationales.B: Background: Clinton signed major Republican-backed measures, including welfare reform in 1996.
rationales.C: Background: Clinton served out both terms and won reelection in 1996.
rationales.D: Background: Clinton never proposed a constitutional amendment against the Contract; he co-opted its agenda instead.
rationales.general:
1. Picture Clinton after 1994: a Democratic president facing a Republican Congress for the first time in forty years.
2. Background: instead of fighting on the left, he moved to the center — declaring the era of big government over and signing welfare reform.
3. Background: by embracing NAFTA and welfare reform, he took the Republicans' own issues and made them his.
4. He did not veto everything, resign, or chase an amendment — he triangulated.
Remember: Clinton answered 1994 by moving to the center, not by digging in.

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the Contract with America (1994). Post-1929 material is paraphrased, not quoted.
stimulus.text: Paraphrase of the Contract with America, issued by House Republicans six weeks before the 1994 midterm elections: Led by Minority Leader Newt Gingrich, House Republicans promised a package of measures including tougher crime laws, welfare reform, tax cuts, and limits on Congress itself. They presented it as a pledge they would act on in the first hundred days of the new Congress.
